name: Charging a plate
description: The top deflection plate is connected to its power supply through a resistor R. A plate is a capacitor: its charge has to flow in through R, so its potential rises as $V(t) = V_s(1 - e^{-t/RC})$ towards the supply's $V_s$, with the time constant $\tau = RC$, here about 8 (C comes from the plates' shape). The ions cross the plates while it is still charging: the Circuits panel shows V(t), with the launch marked. Set the supply so that the beam lands in the detector.

reality.represents: An RC circuit charging a deflection plate

remarks.detail: Its capacitance comes from its shape (the boundary elements); its voltage rises as V_s(1 − e^(−t/RC)), so a beam passing early sees part of it. In an oscilloscope the plates charge in nanoseconds, which limits how fast a signal it can follow.

Resistors, capacitors, inductors and switches are ideal; the leads have no resistance, inductance or delay, and the circuit acts on the plate as if the field spread instantly (quasi-static, here exact: the motion is Newtonian).

remarks.line: Real plates and their fringe fields
remarks.detail: The electrodes are metal boxes standing on the plane, their surface charge solved exactly (boundary elements): uniform between plates, bulging out past their ends, and rearranging when charges come near, as in a real instrument.

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
